subjects.title: Build-time interfaces, entry points and delivery routes
learn: Claude Team adds admin controls, SSO/SAML, domain capture and a no-training commitment; Enterprise adds SCIM, configurable retention, audit logs, Compliance API and a HIPAA-ready option with a BAA.
API and SDK are the same entry point with different ergonomics; the Anthropic SDK does not run an agent loop. The Agent SDK is the managed loop that powers Claude Code, embedded in your own product.
MCP is a sharing convention across clients, not an alternative to API tool use; with only one client it adds overhead without payback.
Claude Code is built for developer workflows and is not a backend for multi-tenant or customer-facing products; use the API, client SDK or Agent SDK.
Four delivery routes (first-party, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry) are chosen by cloud commitments, procurement and identity, not capability. CSP routes lag on new features; model IDs differ.
Skills attach through container.skills and /v1/skills and need the Code Execution Tool. The entry point should follow the work, not precede it.
traps: SDK equals agent loop: the Anthropic SDK is only a typed wrapper over the API; the loop is still your code. The Agent SDK is the one that runs it.
MCP as default: treating MCP as the integration layer for everything, or as a rival to API tool use, when only one client needs the tools.
Claude Code everywhere: reaching for it on non-engineering work or as the engine of a customer-facing product.
Capability-based route choice: picking Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry for model quality, when the model is the same and commitments decide.
Feature parity assumption: assuming CSP routes ship new features the day first-party does, or share model identifiers.

questions.stem: An engineer proposes adopting the Anthropic Python SDK 'so we do not have to write the agent loop'. Which statement about the SDK is accurate?
options: It wraps the API with typed helpers, but any agent loop is still the partner's own code
It is a separate entry point whose model behaviour differs from the direct API
It runs a managed loop that iterates tool calls and handles termination until completion
It supplies the same iteration and stop logic that powers Claude Code in partner apps
questions.explanation: The SDK is a convenience wrapper over the same API entry point; it handles authentication, retries, streaming and tool-use boilerplate but runs no agent loop. The managed loop belongs to the Agent SDK.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to work across many turns inside their own web application, with iteration, tool execution and termination handled for them. Which build-time interface fits best?
options: An MCP server, since it manages the agent loop for every connected client
The Agent SDK, which runs the managed loop used by Claude Code from your own code
The Anthropic Python SDK, which handles tool use and keeps iterating until the task is done
The direct API, since it already includes iteration and termination handling for you
questions.explanation: The Agent SDK is the managed runtime for multi-turn tool use embedded in your own product. The Anthropic SDK only reduces boilerplate, and MCP shares tools across clients rather than running a loop.
questions.mnemonic: Many turns in my app? Agent SDK.

questions.stem: One internal support app is the only client that will ever use three custom tools. A colleague insists on building an MCP server for them. What is the best response?
options: Build the MCP server, because MCP replaces API tool use as the standard calling convention
Use API tool use directly, because MCP's reuse benefit is absent and adds overhead
Build the MCP server, because MCP is the default integration layer for any tool
Move the tools to the Agent SDK, because MCP cannot run inside a single product
questions.explanation: MCP is a sharing convention across clients. When tools live inside one product only, raw API tool use is the better choice and MCP adds protocol overhead and harder debugging.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about MCP and API tool use are accurate? Select TWO.
options: MCP is an alternative that replaces API tool use in a single product
MCP is required whenever Claude calls any tool
MCP removes debugging complexity compared with direct function calls
An MCP server exposes tools that clients then call using API tool use
MCP is a convention for sharing tools across multiple Claude clients
questions.explanation: MCP and API tool use operate at different layers: MCP exposes and discovers tools across clients, and the calls themselves still use API tool use. MCP actually makes tool-call debugging more complex, not simpler.
questions.mnemonic: MCP shares; API tool use calls.

questions.stem: A startup plans to run Claude Code behind its customer-facing, multi-tenant support portal because it already works well for their developers. What should the architect recommend?
options: Keep Claude Code but assign each tenant a separate permission mode to provide proper isolation
Build on the Claude API, client SDK or Agent SDK, since Claude Code targets developer workflows
Switch to Claude Cowork, which is the supported backend for customer-facing products
Keep Claude Code and add hooks, since the governing layers make it multi-tenant safe
questions.explanation: Claude Code is not designed as a backend for multi-user or customer-facing products. Product integrations should use the API, SDK or Agent SDK. Hooks and permission modes do not change its intended use.
questions.mnemonic: Devs use Claude Code; customers get the API.

questions.stem: What is the strongest reason not to choose Claude Code as the engine of a customer-facing product?
options: It is only available through the Bedrock and Vertex delivery routes, not first-party
It targets developer workflows rather than serving as a multi-tenant or customer-facing backend
It offers no permission boundaries or sandboxing options for production use at all
It cannot read or edit any files outside a single repository directory on the machine
questions.explanation: The notes state plainly that Claude Code targets developer workflows and is not meant for multi-tenant products. It does have permission boundaries and hooks, and it is not route-restricted.
questions.mnemonic: Claude Code: developer desk, not customer door.

questions.stem: A partner has a committed AWS enterprise agreement, uses IAM everywhere and wants AI spend to draw down against that commitment. Which delivery route is usually easiest, and why?
options: Foundry, because Entra ID federates with IAM at no extra effort or cost
The first-party API, because it always offers the strongest model capability on any route
Bedrock, because spend, identity and audit inherit from the existing AWS agreement
Vertex AI, because it provides the broadest regional availability of any delivery route
questions.explanation: Routes are chosen by what the partner has already committed to, not by capability: the model behaves the same on each. AWS contract plus IAM points to Bedrock.
questions.mnemonic: Where you've signed, there you route.

questions.stem: What should primarily decide among the Anthropic first-party, Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry delivery routes?
options: Differences in reasoning quality between the model versions on each route
Which route supports the largest context-window behaviour for long documents
Whether prompting and evaluation strategy can transfer between the routes
Existing cloud commitments, procurement contracts and the partner's identity system
questions.explanation: The model, prompting, evaluation strategy, tool use and context behaviour are the same across routes. What differs is the wrapper: billing, identity, region and procurement.

questions.stem: A partner on Vertex AI asks why a feature announced by Anthropic last week is not yet available to them. What is the most consistent explanation?
options: Cloud routes tend to lag the first-party API on new features by weeks
The partner's prompts must be rewritten for Vertex before features unlock
The feature needs a Claude Enterprise plan before it works on Vertex
Vertex serves a weaker model variant that has different tool-use behaviour
questions.explanation: Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry typically trail the first-party API on new features. Prompting and tool use transfer unchanged, so the lag is a delivery matter, not a model difference.
questions.mnemonic: Cloud routes trail the launch day.

questions.stem: When the same Claude model is reached through a different delivery route, which TWO things change? Select TWO.
options: Context-window behaviour of the model
Model identifiers and version strings
Regional availability and CSP-side wrapper features
The prompting strategy needed for equivalent results
Tool-use semantics inside a single request
questions.explanation: Identifiers, regional availability and wrapper concepts (inference profiles, model deployments, Model Garden controls) differ. Prompting, evaluation, tool use and context behaviour all transfer.

questions.stem: A GDPR-sensitive partner wants to deploy Claude on Microsoft Foundry. Foundry offers Hosted on Azure and Hosted on Anthropic infrastructure forms. What should the architect do?
options: Assume all Foundry models run inside the partner's Azure environment by default
Assume Entra ID authentication guarantees EU residency for every deployed model
Choose the Anthropic-infrastructure hosting form because it is generally available
Verify the hosting form and compliance posture of each specific model first
questions.explanation: Only the Hosted on Azure form runs inference in the partner's Azure environment; other models route to Anthropic-managed infrastructure. Residency claims must be checked per model.
questions.mnemonic: Foundry: check where inference actually runs.

questions.stem: A team attaches a versioned Skill to requests via container.skills and publishes it through /v1/skills. What dependency does this integration carry?
options: The Code Execution Tool, which provides a sandboxed execution environment
An MCP server hosting the Skill for every connected client
A Bedrock inference profile used to version the Skill
The Agent SDK, which must run the Skill's managed loop
questions.explanation: Skills are an integration mechanism that require the Code Execution Tool to run, adding a sandboxed execution dependency to the pattern.

questions.stem: A firm already has SSO and now needs SCIM provisioning, configurable retention, audit logs and a Compliance API on Claude.ai. Which tier provides these?
options: Team, which adds SCIM and the Compliance API on top of its existing admin controls
Pro, which adds audit logs for individual users and for small teams as well
Max, which adds configurable retention for shared Projects and uploaded files
Enterprise, adding SCIM, configurable retention, audit logs, Compliance API and a BAA option
questions.explanation: Team adds admin controls, SSO/SAML, domain capture and a no-training commitment. SCIM, retention settings, audit logs, Compliance API and the HIPAA-ready BAA option are Enterprise.
questions.mnemonic: Team has SSO; Enterprise has SCIM and audit.

questions.stem: Which TWO are described as the most common entry point mistakes? Select TWO.
options: Using the SDK instead of raw HTTP for typed helpers
Choosing the Agent SDK when a managed loop is needed
Treating MCP as the default integration layer regardless of reuse needs
Reaching for Claude Code on non-engineering work
Picking a delivery route by existing cloud commitment
questions.explanation: The entry point should follow the work. Claude Code suits engineering, and MCP only pays back when tools are shared across clients. The other options are sound choices.

questions.stem: Operations staff who are not developers need Claude to manage files and tasks directly on their own computers. Which entry point is the best fit?
options: Claude in Chrome, since it automates file management across the desktop
Claude for Excel, since spreadsheets hold most operations task data
Claude Code, since it is the only entry point that can act on local files
Claude Cowork, the desktop agent for non-developers working with local files and applications
questions.explanation: Cowork targets non-engineering roles needing real system actions on the machine, with permission scoping and human review mattering more. Chrome fits web apps and Excel fits spreadsheets.

subjects.title: RAG: chunking, indexing and retrieval strategy
learn: Chunking follows document structure: fixed-size for homogeneous unstructured text, semantic for self-contained prose, hierarchical for contracts, manuals and policies where section context carries meaning.

Indexing follows query pattern: dense for paraphrase and intent, sparse (BM25) for exact tokens such as part numbers, statute citations and error codes, hybrid for mixed patterns; reciprocal rank fusion merges the lists.
Retrieval trades quality, latency and maintenance; quality is measured against a labelled set because it is invisible in fluent output.
Retrieval is for stable knowledge; live state needs a tool call to the system of record. Similarity is not truth, and a better chunker or shorter refresh does not fix it.
Confident wrong answers after a document refresh with unchanged latency and model point first to retrieval or indexing.

Progressive, just-in-time context is the default for production; monolithic suits bounded tasks and stable cacheable prefixes. RAG fails on split tables or code, top-k recall misses and multi-document synthesis.
traps: Chunk-size default: picking a size rather than matching chunking to document structure.
Dense-only for everything: missing exact identifiers like part numbers or citations that need a sparse or hybrid index.
RAG for live state: stale chunks look fluent and error-free; a better embedding model or faster refresh will not cure it.
Blaming the model: after a refresh, confident wrong answers with unchanged latency and model version point to retrieval first, not temperature or weights.
Monolithic by habit: loading everything works until context accumulates and the working-memory cliff arrives silently.

questions.stem: A legal-tech team indexes contracts and policy manuals where the meaning of a clause depends on its section and subsection. Which chunking approach fits best?
options: One chunk per entire document, so that no section is ever split apart by the chunker
Fixed-size chunking with overlap, because it is the simplest approach to operate and tune
Hierarchical chunking that preserves sections and subsections and retrieves at the fitting level
Semantic chunking only, splitting on topic shifts while ignoring document headings
questions.explanation: Hierarchical chunking suits structured documents where section context carries meaning. Fixed-size ignores structure and cuts across clauses.

questions.stem: Which TWO pairings of chunking approach and corpus are well matched? Select TWO.
options: Fixed-size chunking for structured policies where section hierarchy carries the meaning
Hierarchical chunking for flat unstructured chat transcripts
Hierarchical chunking for contracts and manuals where section context carries meaning
Fixed-size chunking with overlap for homogeneous unstructured text with weak natural boundaries
Semantic chunking for tabular price lists with rigid column layouts
questions.explanation: Chunking is chosen by the structure of the source, not a default size. Fixed-size is the simple choice for homogeneous text; hierarchical keeps structure for sectioned documents.

questions.stem: Users search a parts catalogue with queries like 'KX-4410-B gasket' and a dense-only index keeps returning semantically similar but wrong parts. What change best addresses this?
options: Shorten the index refresh interval so new part numbers appear sooner
Add a sparse BM25 index beside the dense one as a hybrid
Raise the embedding model's dimensionality while keeping a dense-only index
Switch to larger fixed-size chunks so each result carries more context
questions.explanation: Queries hinging on exact tokens such as part numbers need keyword matching. Hybrid recovers the exact-match results dense retrieval misses while keeping semantic recall.

questions.stem: Which query pattern most clearly justifies adding sparse (keyword) retrieval to a dense index?
options: Lookups of statute citations and error codes that depend on specific tokens
Questions paraphrased very differently from the wording of the source text
Broad conceptual questions about user intent and general themes
Requests about the current status of a customer's order
questions.explanation: Sparse methods such as BM25 match exact terms and identifiers. Paraphrase and concept matching is the dense index's strength, and live order status is not a retrieval problem at all.
questions.mnemonic: BM25 for IDs, dense for ideas.

questions.stem: Employees ask HR questions in casual wording that rarely matches the formal policy text. Which indexing strategy handles this pattern best on its own?
options: Fixed-size chunking with no embedding index of any kind
Dense embeddings, which match meaning rather than exact words
Sparse keyword search combined with a much larger top-k setting
Sparse BM25, which matches paraphrased intent instead of shared terms
questions.explanation: Dense indexes capture semantic similarity, which suits queries phrased differently from the source. Sparse retrieval depends on shared terms.

questions.stem: A hybrid index returns one dense ranked list and one sparse ranked list. Which approach is the standard low-tuning way to merge them?
options: Retraining the embedding model on the sparse list's top-ranked results
Averaging the raw similarity scores from both lists into one number
Reciprocal rank fusion, which scores by rank so items strong in both lists rise
Keeping only the dense list whenever the two lists disagree on order
questions.explanation: Reciprocal rank fusion works on ranks, favoring items that rank well in both lists, and gives a defensible default for combining dense and sparse results.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the retrieval design trade-off?
options: Hybrid indexing improves retrieval quality while also lowering both latency and ongoing maintenance effort
Smaller chunks and hybrid indexing raise quality and latency together; large dense-only designs trade quality for speed
Dense-only retrieval with large chunks maximises quality at essentially no added cost to the team
Smaller chunks lower latency and raise maintenance cost without any change in quality at all
questions.explanation: The three-way trade-off among quality, latency and maintenance has no universal answer; choose the point that fits the corpus and queries, and be able to defend it.
questions.mnemonic: Quality, latency, upkeep: pick two to lean.

questions.stem: A RAG system produces fluent answers, but the team cannot tell whether the right chunks are being retrieved. How should retrieval quality be assessed?
options: Increase top-k until the answers stop looking wrong to the human reviewers
Measure it against a labelled set, since poor retrieval is invisible in output
Read a sample of the final answers and check them carefully for fluency and tone
Track the latency and error-rate dashboards for retrieval calls over time
questions.explanation: The failure mode is a confident answer built on the wrong chunk, which looks fine. Retrieval quality must be evaluated directly against labelled data.
questions.mnemonic: Fluent is not found: label and measure.

questions.stem: A retail assistant answers 'Where's my order?' from an index and cites two contradictory snapshots, one saying shipped and one saying processing. What is the correct fix?
options: Shorten the index refresh interval to hourly so snapshots stay closer to current
Use a better chunker so the two conflicting snapshots are merged together cleanly
Call the order-status service for live state; keep only stable FAQ content indexed
Raise the similarity threshold so that the weaker chunk is dropped
questions.explanation: Order status is live state owned by a system of record. An index holds historical snapshots, so no retrieval tuning can make it current; a tool call can.

questions.stem: An assistant gives stale, confident answers about inventory levels pulled from a vector index. Which TWO changes are appropriate? Select TWO.
options: Move to a more accurate embedding model for the vector index
Query the inventory system directly with a tool call
Shorten the index refresh interval so inventory updates arrive sooner
Raise the similarity threshold applied to retrieved chunks
Keep stable product manuals and FAQs in the retrieval index
questions.explanation: Retrieval is for stable knowledge; tool use is for live state. Better embeddings, faster refresh or thresholds still leave the answer a snapshot of past text.
questions.mnemonic: Index the manual, query the stock.

questions.stem: In the order-tracking trace, the model merged two stale chunks into a confident answer. What principle does this illustrate?
options: Higher similarity scores guarantee that the most recent snapshot is always selected
Hybrid indexing would have flagged which of the two snapshots was current
Embedding similarity measures closeness to the query, not whether text is current
Smaller chunks would have exposed the conflict between the two snapshots to the model
questions.explanation: The index conflated two snapshots that were each true at a different time. Similarity cannot identify which is current, and the actual current state appeared in neither chunk.

questions.stem: After a document refresh, a RAG assistant gives confident but incorrect answers while latency and model version are unchanged. What is the most likely first place to investigate?
options: A temperature setting that has been configured too low for the task
A context window that has shrunk since the document refresh
The model weights having silently changed overnight without any announcement
Retrieval and indexing returning irrelevant or stale chunks, such as a broken re-index
questions.explanation: A document refresh specifically touches retrieval and indexing. With model and latency unchanged, poor or stale context is the likeliest cause; the other options would not be triggered by a refresh.
questions.mnemonic: Refresh broke it? Check the index.

questions.stem: Which TWO are documented ways that retrieval-based context fails? Select TWO.
options: Chunking splits semantic units such as tables or code blocks
The correct document never enters the top-k results
Citations can never be produced from retrieved source documents
Retrieval removes the need to evaluate or maintain the pipeline
Queries needing synthesis across many documents are its strongest use case
questions.explanation: RAG breaks on split units, recall misses and cross-document synthesis because chunks are scored independently. It also creates a retrieval system that must be evaluated and maintained.
questions.mnemonic: Split tables, missed top-k, lonely chunks.

questions.stem: A long-running agent loop accumulates tool output and history every turn, and the window fills silently. Which context strategy is the better default?
options: Retrieval alone, with no summarising or compaction of any of the earlier steps
Monolithic context that reloads the entire history and the full corpus on every call
A larger monolithic prompt sized to fill the maximum context window available
Progressive context: retrieve just in time and carry forward only what the next step needs
questions.explanation: Monolithic context hits the working-memory cliff as context accumulates. Progressive staging is the default for most production workloads, often layered with retrieval and compaction.
questions.mnemonic: Stage the context; don't dump it.

questions.stem: For which situation is a monolithic context strategy a reasonable choice?
options: A tool loop where each step depends mainly on the most recent state
A multi-turn conversation whose history keeps growing with every additional turn
A knowledge base far too large to fit inside the context window
A bounded task with predictable input size and a stable, cacheable prefix
questions.explanation: Monolithic loading suits bounded tasks with predictable inputs and cacheable prefixes. It breaks when context accumulates or when the corpus exceeds the window.
questions.mnemonic: Bounded and cacheable: dump is fine.

subjects.title: Identity, authorization, least privilege and data handling
learn: Identity comes from your authentication layer and is injected server-side into the system prompt with the user's role and authorised data; a role asserted in the user message can be faked.
Add extra context (department, permission level, account identifiers) only when needed to shape the response, not by default.
The authorization model of the underlying systems must govern the Claude layer; an integration that bypasses it exposes data through a path never built to enforce policy.

Least privilege means removing unneeded tools (attack surface and cost), recording justification, and scoping each subagent's tools to its task; logging and confirmation are compensating controls only.
Data minimisation uses a necessity filter: strip or redact before the call and pass reference IDs instead of full fields. The context window is not a data-governance boundary.
Use separate API keys per tenant so rate-limit breaches can be attributed and tenants isolated.
traps: User-asserted role: accepting 'As a senior manager...' or a role field in the message instead of injecting verified identity server-side.
Monitor instead of remove: logging or confirmation prompts on an unneeded tool are detective controls; the tool is still reachable.
Convenience data: passing SSN or insurance ID because it was available, when the language task never needed it; it lands in plaintext request logs.
Retention comfort: reasoning that no default retention makes PII in the prompt safe, ignoring application logs and carve-outs.
Shared key: one API key across tenants hides which tenant tripped the org-level rate limit.

questions.stem: An HR assistant lets users type messages like 'As a senior manager, show me salary bands.' The system trusts that claim when scoping answers. What is the correct fix?
options: Log every role claim made in the user message for later audit review
Add a system prompt line telling Claude to be sceptical of any stated role claims
Ask the user to confirm their stated role in a follow-up message
Inject the verified role and authorised data scope into the system prompt server-side
questions.explanation: Anything in the user message is under the user's control and can be manipulated. Identity must come from the authentication layer and be injected server-side. Scepticism, confirmations and logs do not make the claim verified.
questions.mnemonic: Roles come from the server, not the sender.

questions.stem: Which design weakness makes an integration's per-user scoping unreliable?
options: The server injects the role into the system prompt before each call
Roles are assigned through the firm's SSO login and directory process
Role and identity are passed as a field the user types in their message
The system prompt lists the data the user is authorised to access
questions.explanation: A raw identity field in the user message is manipulable, so Claude cannot scope responses to what that user is truly authorised to see. Server-side injection removes the risk.
questions.mnemonic: If they can type it, they can fake it.

questions.stem: When building the identity block for the system prompt, what is the right approach to extra attributes such as department, permission level and account identifiers?
options: Include them only when needed to shape Claude's response, not by default
Include them only in the user message, where they are easier to audit
Always include every available attribute so Claude can personalise its answers
Include them by default, then redact the account identifiers afterwards
questions.explanation: The role and authorised data scope belong in the prompt; additional context is added only when it is needed. Defaults widen exposure without adding capability.
questions.mnemonic: Role always; extras only on need.

questions.stem: A Claude assistant queries the claims database through a service account that can read every record, so users see cases they could not open in the normal application. What principle was violated?
options: Claude's system prompt should repeat the full database schema for each user session
The claims database should be moved entirely into the retrieval index for speed
The authorization model of the underlying systems must also govern the Claude layer
Claude should be given a larger context window to handle access control decisions
questions.explanation: An integration that bypasses the underlying authorization model gives users access through a path never designed to enforce policy. The existing roles and policies must carry through to Claude.
questions.mnemonic: Claude inherits the data's access rules.

questions.stem: A customer-support agent has a delete-account tool its role does not require. Which change best applies least privilege?
options: Switch the agent to a smaller and cheaper model tier instead
Log every call to the delete-account tool for later security review and follow-up
Remove the tool from the agent's configuration, eliminating that attack surface
Add a confirmation prompt before the tool is allowed to execute
questions.explanation: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need. Logging and confirmation are detective or compensating controls that leave the tool reachable, and model size is unrelated to authorization scope.
questions.mnemonic: Don't guard the door; remove it.

questions.stem: Why are confirmation prompts an inadequate substitute for removing an unneeded tool?
options: They make the tool slower to use but equally safe in effect
They compensate for the risk, but the tool stays reachable as attack surface
They apply only to subagents and never to top-level agents
They become redundant once detailed logging has been enabled
questions.explanation: Compensating controls manage the risk of a tool that stays connected. Removal eliminates the exposure entirely, which is the stronger control.
questions.mnemonic: Confirm, log, or cut: cutting wins.

questions.stem: Which TWO practices belong in a least-privilege tool audit for an orchestrator-worker system? Select TWO.
options: Rely on the system prompt alone to tell subagents which tools to avoid
Scope each subagent's tools to the task it performs
Record the justification for every tool removed from the configuration
Give every subagent the orchestrator's full tool set for maximum flexibility
Keep convenient tools because they cost nothing when unused
questions.explanation: Ask for each tool whether it is essential or merely convenient, remove the out-of-scope ones and document why, and set the trust hierarchy by limiting subagent access to what the job needs.

questions.stem: A team connects twenty tools to an agent that uses only five 'just in case'. What is the main problem with the extra fifteen?
options: Unused tools cause the agent loop to keep running without ever terminating
Unused tools permanently reduce the usable size of the model's context window
Each connected tool is a cost and an attack surface, even if rarely called
Unused tools disable prompt caching across the entire system and every request
questions.explanation: Every tool connected to a Claude system adds cost and attack surface. Audit the set as you would permissions and drop what is merely convenient.
questions.mnemonic: Every extra tool: more cost, more surface.

questions.stem: A patient-intake summariser sends name, DOB, SSN and insurance ID in the user message, though the summary needs only concerns, medications and allergies. What is the right redesign?
options: Move the full intake form into the system prompt instead of the user message
Keep the data but tell Claude in the system prompt not to repeat the SSN
Redact non-essential PII server-side before the call and supply only needed fields
Rely on Anthropic's default non-retention and leave the design unchanged
questions.explanation: Necessity is the filter: if the field is not needed for the language task it should not be in the context window. A prompt instruction does not stop the application's request logs capturing it.

questions.stem: A claims workflow needs a claim number only to route a case to the right queue. How should it enter the Claude call?
options: As a reference identifier, without attaching the full claimant data fields
As a retrieved document that is included in every single call by default
As the full claim record, so Claude has the maximum possible context for routing
As part of a user-typed message so that every value can be audited later
questions.explanation: Reference IDs are often enough for routing, and passing full fields exposes data to application-layer logging without adding capability.
questions.mnemonic: Pass the pointer, not the payload.

questions.stem: A designer argues that PII in prompts is acceptable because Anthropic does not retain conversation content by default. What is wrong with this argument?
options: The window is no governance boundary: the request still crosses the wire and gets logged
Data in the system prompt is exempt from logging but data in user messages is not
Anthropic retains all conversation content indefinitely by default on the API, so exposure is certain
Retention only matters for non-API entry points such as the Claude.ai chat product
questions.explanation: Non-retention by default does not change that data is transmitted, may be logged by the partner's application layer, and that retention carve-outs exist for some model classes.
questions.mnemonic: Window is a pipe, not a vault.

questions.stem: In the intake trace, where did thousands of exposed SSNs actually turn up during pre-production review?
options: In the model's weights after a routine fine-tuning cycle on customer data completed
In a system prompt cache that is shared across all of the tenants
In plaintext in the application layer's request logs, in the user message field
In the stop reason field that is returned with each Claude response
questions.explanation: The identifiers travelled with the request and the application's own request logging captured them, surfacing in the audit rather than at deployment.
questions.mnemonic: PII in the prompt lives in your logs.

questions.stem: A multi-tenant product uses one shared API key. At peak the org rate limit trips and every tenant slows. What can the team not do?
options: Measure the aggregate request volume at peak
Observe that a traffic spike occurred at all
Attribute the breach to the tenant that caused it
Retry throttled requests using exponential backoff
questions.explanation: A shared key makes the spike visible but not its source. Separate keys per tenant give attribution and isolation.

questions.stem: Which TWO outcomes justify separate API keys per tenant in production? Select TWO.
options: Tenants are isolated from one another's usage problems
Rate limits are removed for every tenant on its own key
Rate-limit breaches can be attributed to the responsible tenant
Tenant data is encrypted in the context window automatically
Prompt caching is shared safely across all of the tenants
questions.explanation: Per-tenant keys give attribution and isolation. They do not encrypt context, remove limits or provide shared caching.
questions.mnemonic: Key per tenant: blame and boundary.

subjects.title: Regulated-industry constraints on integration
learn: Compliance eliminates entry points and routes before preference. Work in order: governing regulation, surviving entry point and route, integration pattern, then identity, data handling and observability.
Attorney-client privilege: API behind the firm's gateway with SSO, server-assigned identity and a firm-owned audit log of every request.
HIPAA: the BAA must cover the specific configuration in use; beta features are generally excluded unless listed eligible; send only the minimum necessary, using reference IDs where possible.

GDPR and residency: inference_geo supports only 'us' and 'global', so EU pinning needs a cloud route (Bedrock or Vertex); DPA is direct with the API or inherited from the cloud contract; Foundry EU residency is listed as Coming 2026.
FedRAMP: Claude for Government, Bedrock GovCloud, Vertex Assured Workloads. Claude Enterprise on the direct API is not authorised; government environments lag on newest models.
Five integration layers: compliance, identity/SSO, authorization/policy, data handling/PII, observability/audit. This is not legal advice; verify scope with Anthropic.
traps: Pattern before regulation: designing the integration first and discovering later that the route fails BAA, residency or FedRAMP review.
BAA by provider: assuming a BAA held for one configuration, or for beta features, covers the one actually deployed.
inference_geo for EU: assuming it can pin execution to the EU when it only offers 'us' and 'global'.
Enterprise equals FedRAMP: treating Claude Enterprise on the direct API as an authorised substitute for government paths.
Engineering override: replacing the CIO-cleared approved vendor with the technically nicer route; that is procurement, not engineering.

questions.stem: A team is designing an enterprise Claude integration for a regulated client. In what order should decisions be worked through?
options: Observability design, then data handling, then governing regulation, then the delivery route
Governing regulation, then surviving entry point and route, then pattern, then identity and data
Integration pattern, then entry point, then governing regulation, then observability and logging
Preferred model tier, then delivery route, then governing regulation, then identity controls
questions.explanation: Compliance constraints eliminate options before cost, ergonomics or preference enter. Skipping a step risks something that works technically but fails legal or security review.

questions.stem: A team built a working integration, then found during legal review that the chosen route has no BAA coverage for their configuration. Which step was skipped?
options: Adding a second subagent to validate every output the model produces
Selecting a larger context window for the regulated workload before launch
Tuning prompts for the model identifier used on that particular route
Identifying the governing regulation and surviving routes before choosing the integration pattern
questions.explanation: Regulation eliminates entry points and routes first. Redesign after the fact costs the work already invested plus a new architecture.

questions.stem: A law firm wants Claude for privileged document review. Which design is most likely to survive a privilege review?
options: The API called directly from the browser using one key shared across the firm
Claude Code run on each lawyer's laptop in the default permission mode
Consumer-tier Claude.ai accessed through shared team accounts across the whole practice group
The API behind the firm's own application, with SSO and a firm-approved logging gateway
questions.explanation: Privilege review turns on the firm owning the audit trail end to end. A gateway holding the key, enforcing access and logging every request provides that; consumer tiers cannot be audited by the firm.

questions.stem: Which TWO properties make the gateway pattern suitable for attorney-client privilege? Select TWO.
options: The gateway produces an audit log the firm owns
Server-assigned identity and permissions, not claimed by users
Privileged content bypasses the gateway for speed
Anthropic holds the audit log on behalf of the firm
Users choose their own permission scope at login
questions.explanation: The gateway holds the API key, enforces access, and records every request and response retained under firm policy. Identity is server-assigned via SSO.
questions.mnemonic: Own the log, assign the identity.

questions.stem: A health startup signed a BAA covering one Claude configuration but wants to use another route for a new feature. What is the implication?
options: The existing BAA automatically extends to every route from the same provider
A BAA is unnecessary whenever no patient names appear in the data
Only the model name needs to appear anywhere in the signed BAA
The BAA must cover the specific configuration; an uncovered route is ruled out
questions.explanation: A BAA for one configuration does not extend to another. HIPAA-eligible paths include the Claude API with a signed BAA, Bedrock and Vertex, but only the covered configuration counts.
questions.mnemonic: BAA covers the config, not the brand.

questions.stem: A hospital team on a BAA-covered configuration wants to enable a beta feature. What should the architect check first?
options: Nothing, because beta features inherit the account's existing BAA coverage automatically and fully
Whether that beta feature is listed as eligible; betas are generally excluded
Whether the beta feature measurably improves response latency for the clinicians using it
Whether the beta feature is available on the Bedrock delivery route only
questions.explanation: BAA existence is not enough; feature eligibility matters. Beta features are generally excluded unless explicitly listed.

questions.stem: For a PHI workflow, which data-handling approach matches the notes?
options: Strip PHI to what the task requires before the call, using reference IDs
Redact PHI only in the model's response, after the output is generated
Send the full patient record so Claude has complete clinical context for every request
Send full records but disable all application request logging to limit exposure
questions.explanation: Access to PHI is limited to the minimum necessary, applied before the API call is made.

questions.stem: A deployment has an EU data-residency requirement. Which option fits?
options: Claude Code with a local region flag configured at startup of each session
The direct API with inference_geo set to the global value to cover all regions
A pinned-region cloud route such as Bedrock or Vertex, since inference_geo lacks EU
The direct API with inference_geo set to an EU region value for the deployment
questions.explanation: inference_geo currently supports only 'us' and 'global', so EU pinning needs a cloud route. Global does not pin a region.

questions.stem: A colleague says the team can satisfy EU pinning by setting inference_geo on the direct API. What is wrong with that plan?
options: inference_geo pins data at rest but cannot pin inference
inference_geo is valid only on Foundry deployments of the model
inference_geo requires a signed FedRAMP authorisation before it will function
inference_geo accepts only 'us' and 'global', so it cannot pin EU execution
questions.explanation: EU pinning is not available through inference_geo; where there is an EU residency requirement, use a cloud route instead.
questions.mnemonic: inference_geo: US or global, never EU.

questions.stem: How does the data processing agreement differ between using the Claude API directly and using a cloud route?
options: Direct API DPAs are issued by the cloud provider, not Anthropic
Direct API: DPA with Anthropic; cloud route: terms inherited from the cloud contract
Both routes always use the same Anthropic-issued DPA terms
Cloud routes require no DPA of any kind with the provider
questions.explanation: With the Claude API the DPA is with Anthropic directly; with Bedrock or Vertex the terms are inherited from the existing cloud contract.

questions.stem: A partner needs EU data pinning and proposes Microsoft Foundry. What is the right caution?
options: Foundry is the only route that supports EU pinning at present
Foundry EU residency is listed as Coming 2026 with no timeline; verify first
Foundry EU residency is already fully available for every Claude model
Foundry inherits EU pinning from Entra ID without extra configuration
questions.explanation: The notes list Foundry EU residency as Coming 2026 with no confirmed timeline, so availability must be verified before relying on it.

questions.stem: An agency asks whether Claude Enterprise on the direct API can serve a FedRAMP workload. What is the correct answer?
options: No; use Claude for Government, Bedrock GovCloud or Vertex Assured Workloads
Yes, provided a BAA has been signed with Anthropic first
Yes, because Enterprise includes audit logs, SSO and a Compliance API for agencies
Yes, but only for unclassified workloads on the direct API
questions.explanation: Claude Enterprise on the direct API is not FedRAMP authorised and cannot substitute for the authorised paths.

questions.stem: A government team chooses an authorised environment and then asks for the newest commercial model. What should the architect expect?
options: Government routes use a different and older model family entirely
Government environments lag on models, so confirm the route's available model first
The newest model is always available there at the same time
The model lag only ever affects the Foundry route
questions.explanation: Authorised government environments receive the newest models after commercial release, so check availability on the specific route.

questions.stem: A company's internal policy limits Claude to its CIO-cleared cloud vendor, but engineering prefers the direct API for new features. What decides?
options: The route that the engineering team benchmarks highest across all workloads
The route with the earliest availability of newly shipped features and models
Whichever route measures the best latency in the team's own benchmarks
The CIO-cleared approved vendor, because it is procurement rather than engineering
questions.explanation: Internal data-residency policy rules out routes outside the approved list regardless of convenience; the right route is the one the CIO has cleared.

questions.stem: Which THREE are among the five layers of an enterprise Claude integration? Select THREE.
options: Model tier selection
Prompt caching design
Identity and SSO
Compliance and regulated-industry constraints
Observability and audit logging
questions.explanation: The five layers are compliance, identity/SSO, authorization/policy, data handling/PII, and observability/audit. Model tier and caching are separate decisions.

questions.stem: How should an architect treat the constraint-to-integration matrix?
options: A replacement for the firm's own privilege review process
A certification that every listed pattern is automatically compliant
Valid indefinitely, since authorisations never change over time
Guidance to verify with Anthropic and legal counsel, not legal advice
questions.explanation: The notes state it is not legal guidance and that authorisation scope must be verified with Anthropic before committing.

subjects.title: Claude Code layers and observability for integrations
learn: Shaping layers (CLAUDE.md, Skills, subagents, MCP servers) change what the agent knows and does; governing layers (hooks, permission boundaries and approval flows, sandboxing) limit what it may touch.
Hooks fire on lifecycle events as deterministic gates the model cannot skip; use them when the guarantee must come from code rather than prompting.
Six permission modes: default, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions. dontAsk suits locked-down CI; bypassPermissions is for containers or CI only.
Sandboxing enforces the boundary in the environment, so approval prompts are not the only backstop.
Log request, response, context and outcome fields; observability is the precondition for enabling agents, and an unlogged action cannot be allowed.
LLM systems fail quietly, so standard error logging misses wrong-but-fluent output; choose MCP over raw API tool use by reuse across clients.
traps: CLAUDE.md as a gate: instructions in a shaping layer can be skipped; only hooks and permissions guarantee behaviour.
Mode mix-ups: bypassPermissions skips every check and belongs in containers or CI only; dontAsk is the locked-down CI mode.
Prompts as sandbox: relying on approval prompts or the agent's judgment when the environment itself should enforce the boundary.
Error-log confidence: green dashboards with no crashes can still hide confident wrong answers.
Logging gaps: enabling an agent surface without checking which actions its audit logs record.

questions.stem: Which THREE belong to the governing group of Claude Code layers rather than the shaping group? Select THREE.
options: Sandboxing and restricted execution
MCP servers for external tools
Permission boundaries and approval flows
CLAUDE.md standing instructions
Hooks on lifecycle events
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md, Skills, subagents and MCP shape what the agent knows and does. Hooks, permissions and approval flows, and sandboxing govern what it is allowed to touch.
questions.mnemonic: Shape what it knows; govern what it touches.

questions.stem: A team requires a lint and secrets scan before every file write. Their CLAUDE.md asks for it, but the agent occasionally skips the step. What is the best fix?
options: Implement the check as a hook, a deterministic gate the agent cannot skip
Move the instruction into a Skill the agent may choose to invoke
Make the CLAUDE.md instruction longer and more emphatic in its tone and wording
Add the instruction to a subagent's system prompt text instead
questions.explanation: When the guarantee has to come from code rather than prompting, use a hook. CLAUDE.md, Skills and subagents are shaping layers and can be skipped.
questions.mnemonic: Hooks are gates; prompts are hopes.

questions.stem: Why can a hook enforce a rule that a CLAUDE.md instruction cannot?
options: It runs as code on lifecycle events, independent of the model following instructions
It is chosen by the model whenever it seems relevant to the task
It is a procedure the agent invokes on demand when it decides to
It is loaded into context at session start like any other standing instructions
questions.explanation: Hooks fire on events such as before or after a tool runs as deterministic gates. CLAUDE.md loads into context and relies on the model complying.

questions.stem: A team runs Claude Code in a locked-down CI pipeline and wants anything outside explicit allow rules to be refused without prompting. Which mode fits?
options: bypassPermissions, which skips all checks so that nothing can block the pipeline run
plan, which locks the session to read-only until a plan is approved
dontAsk, which auto-denies anything that would prompt and runs only allow-listed actions
acceptEdits, which approves file edits and common filesystem commands automatically
questions.explanation: dontAsk is the mode for locked-down CI. bypassPermissions skips all checks and is scoped to containers or CI, not a restriction mode.

questions.stem: Which statement about bypassPermissions is accurate?
options: It uses a classifier to block risky actions before they run
It skips all permission checks and is scoped to containers or CI
It is the recommended default setting for developer laptops
It prompts only for file deletions and nothing else
questions.explanation: bypassPermissions removes every check, so it belongs only where the environment itself contains the blast radius. The classifier belongs to auto mode.

questions.stem: Which TWO descriptions of permission modes are accurate? Select TWO.
options: dontAsk prompts the user once and then remembers the answer given
default mode auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands
auto uses a classifier to approve safe actions and block risky ones
acceptEdits approves every Bash command without ever prompting the user
plan locks the session to read-only until the user approves a plan
questions.explanation: acceptEdits covers file edits and common filesystem commands only, and other Bash commands still prompt. Default asks before each action, and dontAsk denies rather than prompts.

questions.stem: A deployment's wrong actions would have real consequences and the team relies on approval prompts. What is the better design?
options: Add sandboxing so the environment itself enforces filesystem, network and command limits
Rely on logging to detect any misuse after it has occurred in production
Trust the agent's judgment more by writing a much longer CLAUDE.md file
Increase the number of approval prompts shown to the user during a session
questions.explanation: Approval prompts alone are not a sufficient backstop; the environment should enforce the boundary, not only the agent's judgment.

questions.stem: A security reviewer must decide whether to approve an autonomous agent that performs actions on several surfaces. What does the notes' standard imply?
options: Audit logs become optional once deterministic hooks have been installed on the agent
Approval depends only on the model's published accuracy benchmarks and evaluation scores
An action not logged cannot be allowed, so per-surface audit coverage must be checked
Audit coverage is identical across every surface, interface and Anthropic product
questions.explanation: Observability is treated as the precondition for enabling agents. Coverage varies by surface, so verify which agentic actions are recorded.

questions.stem: Which review-checklist item reflects observability as a precondition for agents?
options: Confirm the agent has access to every tool for flexibility
Confirm the system prompt exceeds a minimum required length
Verify which agentic actions the audit logs record on each chosen surface
Confirm the agent is using the largest available context window
questions.explanation: Without a trustworthy audit trail, an autonomous system is not approved to act; coverage differs between surfaces.
questions.mnemonic: Check the log before the launch.

questions.stem: A team wants to record whether the downstream system accepted Claude's output and any rejection signals. Which log category covers this?
options: The outcome category
The response category
The context category
The request category
questions.explanation: The four categories are request (model version, input tokens, prompt id), response (output tokens, latency, stop reason), context (user role, session ID, caching) and outcome (downstream acceptance or rejection).

questions.stem: Which TWO fields belong in the response log category? Select TWO.
options: Session ID
Prompt identifier
Stop reason
Whether caching was applied
Output token count
questions.explanation: Response fields are output token count, latency and stop reason. Prompt identifier belongs to the request; session ID and caching belong to context.

questions.stem: Dashboards show normal latency and no errors, yet customers report subtly wrong answers. What explains why monitoring stayed green?
options: LLM systems fail quietly: wrong but fluent answers slip past error and timeout logging
Latency monitoring reliably detects hallucinated answers in real time, so none exist
The model crashes silently and then recovers before the next call arrives
The context window resets between calls and so hides every earlier error
questions.explanation: An LLM system does not crash when something goes wrong; it returns a subtly incorrect response. Detecting that needs outcome signals and evaluation, not just error logs.
questions.mnemonic: No crash does not mean no wrong.

questions.stem: Why is an LLM-based system harder to debug than a traditional service?
options: Its latency cannot be measured by any of the standard monitoring tools
It always throws an exception whenever it receives unexpected or invalid input
It exposes no stop reason that engineers can inspect after the response
It can give a plausible wrong answer with no error that logging flags
questions.explanation: Standard logging captures errors and timeouts; it cannot see a quietly incorrect answer with real business consequences, hence the outcome field and evals.
questions.mnemonic: Wrong but fluent slips past logs.

questions.stem: The same Linear integration must be reachable from Claude.ai, Claude Code and an internal app. What is the right choice?
options: Build one MCP server and connect it to each client
Run the Agent SDK separately in every client that needs the tools
Write separate raw API tool definitions inside each of the three clients
Embed the tool descriptions in a CLAUDE.md file shared across clients
questions.explanation: MCP pays back when one tool entry point is needed from multiple Claude clients: build once, connect everywhere.

questions.stem: What is the deciding factor between MCP and raw API tool use?
options: Whether the partner has signed a BAA with Anthropic
Which delivery route the partner is already using
How often the tools will be reused across multiple Claude clients
The size of the output returned by the tool
questions.explanation: Choose MCP when tools must be reachable from several clients, and raw API tool use when they live inside one product.
